newsitem.title: USA: California anti-toxic law covers faucets, court says.
newsitem.headline: California anti-toxic law covers faucets, court says.

text.p: The California Supreme Court ruled on Monday that the state's tough anti-toxics law applied to faucets that leach lead into drinking water.

The state's highest court was ruling in a suit filed by California Attorney General Dan Lungren in 1992 against 16 manufacturers and distributors of drinking water faucets sold and used in California.
The court said that, since it decided to review the case, the state had reached settlements with the 16 faucet makers, all of whom had been dropped from the suit.

But the court said it decided to rule anyway because of the legal importance of the issues. It also noted that there were a number of other faucet manufacturers and plumbing suppliers that could be affected by its decision.
Original defendants in the case included leading faucet manufacturers such as American Standard Cos Inc and Black & Decker Corp subsidiary Price Pfister Inc.
Lungren alleged that the faucets contained significant amounts of lead, classified by the state as a toxic chemical, which could leach into drinking water.

He sued under Proposition 65, passed by California voters in 1986, which bars businesses from knowingly discharging chemicals known to cause cancer or birth defects where they would likely pass into any source of drinking water.
Lead is known to cause reproductive harm, neurological damage, learning disabilities and birth defects, according to Lungren's office.
The faucet makers argued that water in the faucet was not a "source of drinking water" within the meaning of the law and that Lungren had therefore not stated a cause of action against them.
Lower courts agreed with the faucet makers. A state appeals court interpreted the law's words to mean lakes, rivers, streams or aqueducts, but not faucets.

After analyzing the meaning of the phrase "source of drinking water," the California Supreme Court overturned the lower courts' decisions and ruled that Proposition 65 did apply to lead from water faucets.

"We conclude that, in light of both the act's language and its purpose, the attorney general is correct in construing it to prohibit the discharge of toxic chemicals into faucet water," the court said in a majority 5-2 decision.
James Meeder, an attorney for Price Pfister, called Proposition 65 ambiguous and said he was disappointed the court decided to interpret it broadly.
Most of the settlements reached by the companies provided that they would eventually sell in California only faucets that leached lead below maximum levels set by the act, the court said.
